issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) specifies a parameterless method checkOrderReady(): void and describes orderMeal calling checkOrderReady() with no arguments. The solution implementation defines checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging) (i.e., it requires a boolean parameter) and orderMeal calls checkOrderReady(true). This parameter mismatch between the specification and the provided solution can confuse students about the expected signature and how to invoke the method.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the specification by changing the solution's checkOrderReady method to have no parameters (checkOrderReady()) and update internal logging to not require a public parameter. Update the call in orderMeal to call checkOrderReady() with no arguments. Alternatively, if a logging parameter is intentionally required, update the problem statement and UML to document checkOrderReady(boolean) so students know the correct signature.

issues.description: The problem statement specifies a method checkOrderReady() with no parameters, but the reference implementation defines checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging). This changes the method signature (same name but different parameters) and creates a mapping barrier: students reading the specification expect to implement or call a no-argument checkOrderReady(), while the solution supplies only a boolean-parameter variant. The mismatch can confuse students about the required API and how checkOrderReady should be invoked from orderMeal.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the solution match the problem specification by providing a no-argument checkOrderReady() method. Options: (1) Add an overload public void checkOrderReady() that delegates to checkOrderReady(boolean) with a default value, or (2) remove the boolean parameter and implement logging via an internal flag or separate debug method. Alternatively, update the problem statement to document the boolean parameter and its purpose so the API is consistent across artifacts.
